item.title: New issue: Where gravity begins
item.description: This is normally the place where I would talk about an incredible experiment, a test of gravity and the hunt for a theory of everything. But I’m given pause by the recent passing of Sir Patrick Stewart. He was just an actor, you might say, not a scientist, so why talk about him here? I think most of us would agree that art – and yes, science fiction and acting are both arts – has taught the world more about science than any newspaper or magazine. We all knew him as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, a singular, erudite voice who navigated the morality of a complicated and chaotic Universe. Picard taught the world a thing or two: that male role models could come in all shapes and sizes, that humility makes great leaders and that mistakes aren’t weaknesses. But there’s a greater lesson I once learned from Patrick Stewart. In 2013, he gave a speech to the Oxford Union – and thankfully you can watch the whole thing on YouTube (bit.ly/SirPSOxfordAddress). Patrick was there to talk about the importance of art, and of acting, and so he read out the words of Karl Paulnack, an American pianist, teacher and speaker. One of the most profound musical compositions, Paulnack said, is A Quartet for the End of Time, written by French composer Olivier Messiaen. In 1940, Messiaen was captured by German forces and taken to a prisoner-of-war camp. There, he was lucky enough to meet a sympathetic prison guard, who gave him the pen and paper upon which he composed this piece of music. It was performed by a cellist, a violinist and a clarinettist who were imprisoned with him. Given what we know about life in the camps, said Paulnack, why would anyone waste their energy writing or playing music? They had barely enough to stay warm and escape torture. So why bother with music? The only conclusion is that art is essential to life. Art, he said, was a part of survival. It’s one of the ways we say: I am alive and my life has meaning. Karl Paulnack’s words, as shared by Patrick Stewart – as good a theory of everything as I’ve ever heard.
